title: Good feelings
hook: the Stoics kept joy, wise wishing and caution

segments.voice: Yesterday: primus motus, the flinch that comes before anger or fear. Your line was the jolt isn't me. Did you catch the pause before the yes? Day two hundred eighty-seven.

After a week of this, you might be picturing the Stoic as someone with the joy dialed down to zero. Character is the only good. Comforts are just preferred. Feelings have judgments hiding in them. Check the jolt before you agree. It can start to sound like a person who never laughs at a wedding. But the Stoics had a word for the feelings they wanted more of. Not fewer feelings. Better ones. Today, the last day of our week back on the porch: eupatheia.
screen: `JOY DIALED DOWN TO ZERO?` → `NOT FEWER FEELINGS.` → `BETTER ONES.`

segments.voice: Eupatheia is Greek: eu, good or well, plus pathos, the word we met two days ago. So, good feelings. Diogenes Laërtius reports that the Stoics named three, and each one is the healthy twin of a passion. Instead of giddy, grasping pleasure, there's joy: a calm, deep gladness at what's truly good. Instead of craving, there's wishing, wanting something wisely and in the right measure. And instead of fear, there's caution: sensible care about real dangers, like looking both ways without panicking about the traffic. Notice there are three twins for four passions. There's no good version of distress for the fully wise person, because the Stoics thought such a person had nothing truly bad to grieve over. That's one of their hardest claims, and we'll be honest about it in two weeks. Seneca has a lovely line on this in a letter to his friend Lucilius. He says, roughly, believe me, real joy is a serious thing. He means it isn't a sugar rush; it's steady, it comes from inside, and it doesn't vanish when the party ends. The same report lists finer kinds under each: under wishing, goodwill and warm affection; under joy, delight and cheerfulness. So look back at this week. Home to the porch. Arete, character first. The four virtues. Adiaphora, nice not needed. Pathos, and the sentence inside a feeling. Primus motus. And now the good feelings. Put together, the goal was never a cold life. It was a clear one, with room for gladness that no one can take.
screen: `EU + PATHOS: GOOD FEELINGS.` · `JOY, WISHING, CAUTION.` · `REAL JOY IS A SERIOUS THING.` · `THE WEEK ON THE PORCH.` · then, large: `JOY IS ALLOWED.`

segments.voice: Look for one good feeling that's here right now, or was here today. Maybe small: gladness at the light, relief, warmth for someone, the quiet satisfaction of a task done. Find it. Now let it be exactly as big as it is. Don't inflate it, don't wave it away. Rest in it, breathing. The bell holds the time.
Eupatheia. Greek for good feelings: joy, wise wishing and caution, the healthy twins of the passions. Today's word.
Your line: joy is allowed. Notice one good feeling today and let it stay without apology. That's our week back on the porch. Next week, the Stoic world. Day two hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Modern Stoic practitioners distinguish calm joy from excited pleasure and caution from fear, and try to cultivate the steady versions.

fork.setup: a Stoic sees a car coming as she steps off the curb. which good feeling fits?
fork.reveal: caution is the healthy twin of fear: sensible care about a real danger, without panic.

original.note: Greek: good feeling; eu, well, plus pathos, feeling.
